title: Are You Making Your Most Difficult Students Worse? -worse/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explores how heightened teacher vigilance around difficult students can unintentionally worsen their behavior. He explains that hovering, glaring, or tensing up near challenging students communicates that they are viewed as untrustworthy troublemakers, a label they then live up to. The recommended fix is deliberately behaving toward difficult students exactly as one behaves toward the rest of the class—same jokes, same tone, same assumption of good behavior—even though this runs counter to a teacher's natural caution. He acknowledges the strategy is difficult in practice because distrust after repeated disruption feels justified, but insists that consistently pretending difficult students are already well-behaved short-circuits the self-fulfilling prophecy driving their misbehavior. The piece ends on an emotional note, describing students shedding the burden of negative labels and becoming accepted, valued members of the classroom.
points: Visibly treating difficult students differently (glaring, hovering, tensing up) signals distrust and reinforces their troublemaker identity.
Deliberately behave the same way toward difficult students as toward the rest of the class—same warmth, same assumed good behavior.
The strategy requires overriding a natural, understandable instinct toward caution around repeat offenders.
This isn't a claim that misbehavior will vanish entirely, but that it stops being driven by spite or self-fulfilling labels.
As the rest of the class follows the teacher's cue, difficult students gradually shed negative self-labels and integrate as valued classroom members.
quotes: But this awareness can cause you to behave oddly around them.

Because when you act differently around difficult students than you do the rest of your class, you’re effectively telling them that they’re not like other students, that they’re incapable of being trusted and that you expect them to misbehave.
They know when they’re being surveilled, marked, and followed. They know when they’re disliked and resented—or merely tolerated.
The solution, however, is simple: From the very first moment of each school day onward, you’re going to pretend that your most difficult students are already well behaved.
That isn’t to say that they’ll never again misbehave, but they’ll no longer do it to spite you or get under your skin.
Their burden will lift. They’ll look you in the eye, unashamed. And for the first time in their school career, they’ll relax into their skin.
